questions.q: Passage of HIV from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, birth or breast-feeding is called:
questions.x: Transmission from mother to child is called vertical transmission. Spread between unrelated people, for example by sex or shared needles, is horizontal transmission.

questions.q: The HIV envelope glycoprotein gp41 mainly helps the virus to:
o: Bind first to the CD4 receptor
Leave the host cell by lysis
Fuse its envelope with the membrane of the host cell
questions.x: gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein that anchors gp120 and brings about fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane. The first binding to CD4 is done by gp120.

questions.q: The coenzyme NAD+, which carries hydrogen in respiration, is made in the body from the vitamin:
questions.x: NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is built from niacin, a B-group vitamin. Riboflavin is used to make FAD, the other hydrogen carrier.

questions.q: In the overall process of aerobic respiration, which substance is reduced?
questions.x: Glucose loses hydrogen and is oxidized to carbon dioxide, while oxygen gains electrons and hydrogen and is reduced to water.

questions.q: In each turn of the Krebs cycle, how many molecules of ATP (or GTP) are formed directly by substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.x: Each turn yields one ATP (or GTP) by substrate-level phosphorylation, along with three NADH and one FADH2. Most ATP comes later from the electron transport chain.

questions.q: In the straight-chain form of fructose, the carbonyl group is found on:
questions.x: Fructose is a ketose: its carbonyl (C=O) is a ketone group on carbon 2. Glucose, an aldose, has an aldehyde group on carbon 1.

questions.q: Proteins in the cell membrane are important because some of them:
o: Act as channels and carriers for substances moving into and out of the cell
Form the cellulose wall of the cell
Act as the cell's main energy store
questions.x: Membrane proteins form channels and carriers that control the movement of ions and molecules. Hereditary information is in DNA, cellulose forms the wall, and energy is stored in starch, glycogen or fat.

questions.q: In which reaction is water a product rather than a reactant?
o: Hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose
Joining two glucose molecules to form maltose
Splitting of water in the light reaction of photosynthesis
Digestion of proteins into amino acids
questions.x: Forming maltose is a condensation reaction, which releases a water molecule. Hydrolysis, digestion and the splitting of water in photosynthesis all use water.

questions.q: Cotton fibres are made almost entirely of:
questions.x: Cotton is nearly pure cellulose, the structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls.

questions.q: The folded cloverleaf shape of a tRNA molecule is held in place by:
o: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases within the same strand
Peptide bonds between its amino acids
Hydrogen bonds with a second tRNA strand
questions.x: tRNA is a single strand that folds back on itself; complementary bases in its arms pair by hydrogen bonds. It contains no amino acids in its chain and no second strand.

questions.q: The primary structure of a protein is:
o: The coiling of the chain into an alpha helix
The folding of the chain into a three-dimensional shape
The joining of several chains together
The sequence of amino acids in its polypeptide chain
questions.x: Primary structure is simply the order of amino acids. Coiling is secondary structure, overall folding is tertiary, and combining chains is quaternary.

questions.q: The slight ionization of water matters to living things because:
o: It makes water a non-polar solvent
It produces oxygen gas for respiration
It stops water from forming hydrogen bonds
The H⁺ and OH⁻ ions it forms affect pH, and enzymes work only within a narrow pH range
questions.x: Changes in H⁺ concentration change pH, which alters the shape and activity of enzymes and other proteins. Ionization does not produce oxygen or affect water's polarity.

questions.q: When a dipeptide is hydrolysed, a water molecule is split. Which statement correctly describes where its parts go?
o: –H joins the carbon, forming –CHO, and –OH joins the nitrogen, forming –NHOH
–OH joins the carbon of the peptide bond, forming –COOH, and –H joins the nitrogen, forming –NH₂
Both hydrogen atoms join the nitrogen, and the oxygen is released as gas
The whole water molecule attaches to the R group of one amino acid
questions.x: Hydrolysis reverses condensation. The –OH from water restores the carboxyl group of the first amino acid, and the –H restores the amino group of the second.

questions.q: On a hot sunny day, the leaves of a well-watered plant are kept cool mainly because:
o: Evaporation of water during transpiration takes up a large amount of heat
Water in the leaf has a low specific heat
Water in the leaf forms ice crystals that absorb heat
Cellulose in the cell walls reflects all sunlight
questions.x: Water has a high heat of vaporisation, so evaporating water from the leaf removes much heat. This works in the same way as sweating in mammals.

questions.q: How many different tripeptides could, in principle, be made from the 20 kinds of amino acids, if any amino acid can be used at each position?
questions.x: Each of the three positions can hold any of 20 amino acids, so the number is 20 × 20 × 20 = 8000. This shows why proteins can be so varied.

questions.q: The addition of sugar chains to a protein to form a glycoprotein is called:
questions.x: Glycosylation is the attachment of carbohydrate chains to proteins (or lipids). Glycolysis breaks down glucose, and glycogenesis makes glycogen.

questions.q: Which pair of organelles is bounded by a double membrane?
questions.x: The nucleus has a double nuclear envelope and the mitochondrion has outer and inner membranes. Golgi, lysosome, ER and vacuole have single membranes; ribosomes and centrioles have none.

questions.q: Bacteria do not reproduce sexually, but some can transfer DNA from one cell to another through a sex pilus. This process is called:
questions.x: In conjugation, DNA (often a plasmid) passes from a donor to a recipient bacterium through a sex pilus. Binary fission is asexual division, and meiosis does not occur in prokaryotes.

questions.q: The core of a nucleosome contains two molecules each of the histones:
questions.x: The histone octamer is two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. H1 is not part of the core; it binds the linker DNA outside it.

questions.q: Down syndrome usually arises because the parent's gamete carried an extra chromosome 21. This extra chromosome is most often due to:
questions.x: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes or chromatids to separate in meiosis, so a gamete receives two copies of chromosome 21 instead of one.

questions.q: Pancreatic cells are given radioactive amino acids for a few minutes. Shortly afterwards, most of the radioactivity is found first in the:
questions.x: Labelled amino acids are built into proteins on the ribosomes of the rough ER, so the label appears there first and only later in the Golgi and secretory vesicles.

questions.q: Cells of nervous tissue that support, protect and nourish neurons but do not conduct impulses are called:
questions.x: Neuroglia, including Schwann cells, support neurons. Neurofibrils and Nissl's granules are structures inside neurons, not separate cells.

questions.q: The raised ridges on the folded surface of the cerebral cortex are called:
questions.x: The cortex is folded into ridges called gyri, separated by grooves called sulci. Ventricles are cavities inside the brain, and meninges are its covering membranes.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, the sensory neuron synapses with a single interneuron, which synapses with the motor neuron. How many synapses between neurons does this arc have?
questions.x: There is one synapse from sensory neuron to interneuron and one from interneuron to motor neuron, giving two. This makes it a polysynaptic reflex; a monosynaptic arc would have only one.

questions.q: A resting neuron is said to be polarised because:
o: The inside of its membrane is negative compared with the outside
Its Na+ channels are fully open
The inside of its membrane is positive compared with the outside
questions.x: At rest there is a charge difference across the membrane, with the inside negative (about -70 mV). The inside becomes positive only briefly during an action potential.

questions.q: In a section through the cerebellum, the branching, tree-like pattern of white matter is called the:
questions.x: The white matter of the cerebellum branches like a tree inside the grey cortex and is called the arbor vitae ('tree of life'). The corpus callosum joins the cerebral hemispheres.

questions.q: Gentle pressure on a closed eye can make a person 'see' flashes of light. This shows that the sensation felt depends mainly on:
o: The form of energy in the stimulus
The strength of the pressure applied
The number of touch receptors in the eyelid
Which part of the brain receives the impulses
questions.x: All receptors send the same kind of nerve impulse. Pressure that stimulates the retina sends impulses to the visual area, so the brain interprets them as light, whatever the stimulus was.

questions.q: A woman's ears and auditory nerves work normally, but after a stroke damaging both temporal lobes she cannot hear. This is because the temporal lobes contain the:
questions.x: Sound impulses are interpreted in the auditory area of the temporal lobes, so damage there causes deafness even with normal ears. The visual area is in the occipital lobe and the motor area in the frontal lobe.

questions.q: Which statement about the functions of the brainstem is correct?
o: It is the main centre of intelligence and memory
It is responsible for the conscious perception of vision and hearing
It controls vital functions such as breathing and heartbeat and carries tracts between spinal cord and brain
It is the main centre for balance and posture
questions.x: The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) contains vital centres and the nerve tracts linking the spinal cord with higher parts. Intelligence and conscious perception belong to the cerebrum, balance to the cerebellum.

questions.q: Enzymes extracted from cells can still catalyse their reactions in a test tube. This shows that enzymes:
o: Need an intact cell membrane to work
Can act independently of the living cell
questions.x: Enzymes are made by living cells but are only proteins; given suitable conditions they work outside the cell too. This is why digestive enzymes work in the gut cavity.

questions.q: Enzyme inhibitors can be divided into two broad groups:
questions.x: Reversible inhibitors bind by weak bonds and can leave the enzyme; irreversible inhibitors bind permanently, often by covalent bonds.

questions.q: Bacteria that live in hot springs have enzymes that:
o: Have high optimum temperatures and are not denatured at those temperatures
questions.x: Enzymes of such heat-loving (thermophilic) bacteria have very stable structures, so they keep their shape and work best at high temperatures.

questions.q: An enzyme has an optimum temperature because:
o: The enzyme stops moving at the optimum
Activation energy rises as temperature rises
Rising temperature increases collisions but also increases denaturation, and the balance gives the highest rate at the optimum
The substrate is denatured above the optimum
questions.x: Up to a point, faster molecular movement speeds the reaction. Beyond it, denaturation of enzyme molecules outweighs this, so the rate falls.

questions.q: Darwin believed that new species form:
o: Slowly and gradually, over very many generations
Only by the inheritance of acquired characters
questions.x: Darwin's view, influenced by Lyell, was gradualism: small favourable variations accumulate over long periods to produce new species.

questions.q: Which change that arises during an organism's life CAN be passed on to its offspring?
o: A mutation in a cell that will form gametes
A scar formed after an injury
A larger brain from years of study
questions.x: Changes in cells of the germ line can be inherited because they are carried in the gametes. Effects of exercise, injury or training are in body cells only.

questions.q: The oceans of the early Earth formed when:
o: The Earth cooled and water vapour condensed and fell as rain
Ice from comets melted after life began
Photosynthetic cells released water as a product
Underground rivers broke through the crust
questions.x: As the young Earth cooled, water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and fell as rain for long periods, filling low areas to form the first oceans.

questions.q: The idea that living things arise from non-living matter is called:
questions.x: Abiogenesis means life from non-life. Biogenesis is the principle that life comes only from pre-existing life.

questions.q: About how many oocytes are released by ovulation during a woman's entire reproductive life?
questions.x: Although the ovaries contain hundreds of thousands of oocytes at puberty, usually only one is released each cycle, giving roughly 400 over the reproductive years.

questions.q: A man takes large doses of synthetic testosterone-like steroids for body-building. His testes are likely to:
o: Enlarge and produce more sperm, because testosterone is high
Stay unchanged, because steroids act only on muscles
Begin secreting oestrogen instead of testosterone
Shrink and produce fewer sperm, because FSH and LH are suppressed
questions.x: High steroid levels feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH, FSH and LH. Without these, the testes shrink and sperm production falls.

questions.q: During the follicular phase, which ovarian hormone remains at a low level?
questions.x: Progesterone stays low until the corpus luteum forms after ovulation. Oestrogen rises steadily during the follicular phase.

questions.q: The female pelvis is broader and shallower than the male pelvis. This is an adaptation for:
questions.x: The wider female pelvic opening allows the baby's head to pass during birth. It does not make running faster or protect the kidneys.

questions.q: Each Z line of a myofibril anchors thin filaments belonging to:
o: The thick filaments of the same sarcomere
Myofibrils of a neighbouring muscle fibre
questions.x: A Z line is the boundary shared by two sarcomeres, so thin filaments project from it into the sarcomere on each side. Thick filaments are not attached to the Z line; they are held at the M line.

questions.q: A tendon attaches:
questions.x: Tendons connect muscles to bones and transmit the pull of the muscle to the skeleton. Ligaments are the bands that join bone to bone at a joint.

questions.q: Which statement about the control of muscles is correct?
o: Skeletal muscle contracts only when stimulated by somatic motor nerves, but cardiac muscle beats on its own
Cardiac muscle contracts only when stimulated by voluntary nerves
Smooth muscle is controlled by the somatic nervous system
Skeletal muscle is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
questions.x: Skeletal muscle needs impulses from somatic motor neurons. Cardiac muscle is myogenic, and both cardiac and smooth muscle are regulated by the autonomic nervous system.

questions.q: A fracture through the growth plate of a 10-year-old's femur may leave that leg shorter. This is because the growth plate:
o: Is where the blood cells of the leg are made
Is where new cartilage forms and is replaced by bone, lengthening the bone
Attaches the tendons to the bone
Stores calcium for the whole body
questions.x: Growth in length takes place at the epiphyseal plate, where cartilage keeps growing and is turned into bone. Damage there can stop this process, so the bone grows less than the other one.

questions.q: Which comparison of skeletal and smooth muscle is correct?
o: Skeletal muscle is involuntary; smooth muscle is voluntary
Smooth muscle is striated; skeletal muscle is not
Skeletal fibres are multinucleate; smooth muscle cells have one nucleus
questions.x: Skeletal fibres have many nuclei, while each smooth muscle cell has a single central nucleus. Neither is branched, skeletal is voluntary, and only skeletal is striated.

questions.q: A myofibril is 1 cm long and each of its sarcomeres is 2.5 µm long. About how many sarcomeres lie end to end in it?
questions.x: 1 cm = 10 000 µm, and 10 000 ÷ 2.5 = 4000 sarcomeres. Errors in converting centimetres to micrometres give 400 or 40 000.

questions.q: The thin membrane that lines the marrow cavity of a long bone is the:
questions.x: The endosteum lines the inner marrow cavity. The periosteum covers the outer surface of bone, and the perichondrium surrounds cartilage.

questions.q: In Mendel's dihybrid experiment, which seed colour was dominant?
questions.x: Yellow seed colour is dominant over green in peas, which is why all F1 seeds of round yellow × wrinkled green were yellow. Green reappeared only in the F2.

questions.q: Which test result is typical of a person with hemophilia?
o: A very low red blood cell count
questions.x: In hemophilia a clotting factor is missing, so blood takes much longer to clot. The platelet count is usually normal.

questions.q: In a bivalent of an AB/ab dihybrid, a crossover occurs, but outside the region between loci A and B. For these two genes, the chromatids will carry:
o: Two parental and two recombinant combinations
New alleles created by the crossover
questions.x: Only a crossover between two loci separates their alleles. A crossover outside that region keeps the dominant alleles together on one chromatid and the recessive alleles together on the other, so all chromatids stay parental for these genes.

questions.q: Whether a son is colour-blind depends only on:
o: The genotypes of both parents equally
The genotype of his paternal grandfather
questions.x: A son receives his only X from his mother and a Y from his father. So his colour vision is decided by the X he gets from her.

questions.q: For three children of the same parents, what is the probability that at least one will be a son?
questions.x: The chance that all three are daughters is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. So the chance of at least one son is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

questions.q: A woman with normal clotting has a hemophilic father. Her genotype must be:
questions.x: Her father could give her only his Xʰ. Since her clotting is normal, her other X carries Xᴴ, so she is a carrier.

questions.q: The law of independent assortment describes the inheritance of:
o: The two alleles of a single gene
Genes located close together on one chromosome
Characters controlled only by the environment
Two or more different characters controlled by different genes
questions.x: Independent assortment is about how genes for different characters are sorted relative to each other. The separation of the two alleles of one gene is the law of segregation, and closely placed genes on one chromosome are linked.

questions.q: In a family the father has hemophilia and the mother is heterozygous. What is the chance that any son of theirs is affected?
questions.x: A son's X comes only from his mother, who has one Xʰ and one Xᴴ. So each son has a 1/2 chance; the father's allele does not reach sons.

questions.q: A band is tied fairly tightly around the upper arm, and the veins below it swell. This happens because:
o: The band forces blood backwards from the heart into the arm
The arteries below the band burst
Blood still enters through the deep arteries but cannot leave through the squeezed veins
The valves in the arm veins open wider
questions.x: Thin-walled veins are compressed easily, but the deeper high-pressure arteries keep supplying blood. Blood enters and cannot get out, so the veins fill and bulge.

questions.q: Which vein carries oxygenated blood?
questions.x: Pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The other veins carry blood that has already given up oxygen to the tissues.

questions.q: To pump 6 litres each minute at 80 beats, how much blood must one ventricle eject with every beat?
questions.x: Stroke volume = cardiac output ÷ heart rate = 6000 mL ÷ 80 = 75 mL per beat.

questions.q: The narrow space between the two layers of the pericardium is filled with:
questions.x: The pericardial cavity between the two pericardial layers contains a thin film of pericardial fluid, which lets the heart move with little friction. It contains no air or blood.

questions.q: Most antigens are:
o: Large molecules such as proteins and polysaccharides
Small ions such as sodium and chloride
questions.x: Antigens are usually large molecules, chiefly proteins and polysaccharides on the surfaces of pathogens or foreign cells. Small ions and simple sugars do not trigger an immune response.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the:
o: Insulin-secreting beta cells of the pancreas
Red blood cells in the spleen
Helper T cells in the blood
questions.x: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own lymphocytes attack the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans, so little insulin is made. Glucagon comes from alpha cells of the pancreas, not the liver.

questions.q: A lymphocyte is described as immunocompetent when it:
o: Has receptors that let it recognise and respond to one particular antigen
Has lost its nucleus and carries oxygen
Can engulf any pathogen it meets
Is able to divide only once
questions.x: Immunocompetence means the lymphocyte has matured and carries surface receptors for a specific antigen, so it can respond to it. Engulfing any pathogen is the non-specific job of phagocytes.

questions.q: Which is the correct sequence of events in normal quiet expiration?
o: Muscles contract → volume of thorax increases → pressure in lungs falls → air flows out
Muscles relax → volume of thorax increases → pressure in lungs rises → air flows out
Muscles relax → volume of thorax decreases → pressure in lungs rises above atmospheric → air flows out
Muscles contract → volume of thorax decreases → pressure in lungs falls below atmospheric → air flows out
questions.x: In quiet expiration the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the thoracic volume falls, the lungs recoil and the pressure inside them rises above atmospheric, so air moves out. Air always flows from higher to lower pressure.

questions.q: Inside the right lung, the right primary bronchus divides into how many secondary (lobar) bronchi?
questions.x: Each secondary (lobar) bronchus supplies one lobe. The right lung has three lobes, so it has three lobar bronchi; the left lung, with two lobes, has two.

questions.q: Children who grow up in homes where adults smoke indoors are more likely than other children to suffer from:
questions.x: Breathing in other people's smoke irritates children's airways and weakens their defences, so they have more asthma attacks, bronchitis and other chest infections. It does not improve lung growth or capacity.

questions.q: Which statement about the human vermiform appendix is correct?
o: It secretes enzymes that digest cellulose
It has no known digestive role, but it can become inflamed (appendicitis)
It is the main site of water absorption
questions.x: In humans the appendix plays no part in digestion and is regarded as a vestigial organ. If it becomes blocked and infected, it is inflamed: appendicitis.

questions.q: Glucose continues to be absorbed from the ileum even when its concentration in the lumen is lower than in the epithelial cells. This shows that glucose is absorbed by:
questions.x: Moving glucose against its concentration gradient needs carrier proteins and energy, which is active transport. Simple and facilitated diffusion only move substances down a gradient, and osmosis is the movement of water.

questions.q: Fluid filtered out of the glomerular blood crosses which layers, in order, to reach the space inside Bowman's capsule?
o: Podocyte layer → basement membrane → capillary endothelium
Basement membrane → capillary endothelium → podocyte layer
Capillary endothelium → podocyte layer → basement membrane
Capillary endothelium → basement membrane → podocyte layer
questions.x: Filtrate first passes through the pores of the capillary endothelium, then the basement membrane, and finally the slits between the podocytes of the inner capsule wall.

questions.q: Even a person who is very short of water must still pass some urine every day because:
o: The bladder cannot hold urine for more than a day
Urea and other wastes can only be removed dissolved in some water
ADH cannot be secreted during dehydration
Filtration stops completely when water is short
questions.x: The kidneys can concentrate urine only up to a limit, so excreting each day's urea needs a minimum volume of water. Here the excretory role sets a limit on how much water osmoregulation can save.

questions.q: A person with liver disease has a low plasma protein level. In the peritubular capillaries this would:
o: Reduce the osmotic pull that draws reabsorbed fluid into the blood
Increase the uptake of reabsorbed fluid
Raise their hydrostatic pressure above that of the glomerulus
Have no effect, because proteins do not affect water movement
questions.x: Fluid enters the peritubular capillaries mainly because their protein-rich plasma has a high osmotic pressure. With fewer proteins this pull is weaker, so uptake of reabsorbed fluid is reduced.

questions.q: Insects remove uric acid from their body fluid through:
questions.x: Malpighian tubules collect wastes from the body fluid and pass uric acid into the gut, where water is reabsorbed and dry waste is passed out.

questions.q: Hibernation helps some mammals survive winter because:
o: Raising body temperature prevents them from freezing
Lowering body temperature and metabolic rate saves stored energy when food is scarce
questions.x: In hibernation the set point is lowered so far less energy is spent keeping warm, letting stored fat last through the winter.

questions.q: A student compares the male and female urethra. Which of her notes is right?
o: It carries urine from each kidney to the bladder
In females it is longer than in males
It is lined by nephrons that reabsorb water
In males it carries both urine and semen
questions.x: The male urethra runs through the penis and is shared by the urinary and reproductive systems. It is much longer than the female urethra; the ureters, not the urethra, link kidneys to bladder.

questions.q: Small aquatic animals such as Hydra can get rid of ammonia simply by:
o: Diffusion across the body surface into the surrounding water
Storing it as crystals inside the body
Converting it to urea in a liver
questions.x: Ammonia is very soluble and small molecules diffuse rapidly; in a small water-living animal every cell is close to the water, so no special organ is needed.

questions.q: Repeated untreated bacterial infections that spread up from the bladder into the kidneys can lead to:
o: An increase in the number of nephrons
Scarring of the kidneys and eventually kidney failure
questions.x: Infection of kidney tissue causes inflammation and scarring. Scarred nephrons stop working, and repeated damage can end in kidney failure.

questions.q: Compared with the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule, the cells of the distal convoluted tubule have:
o: A thicker brush border, as most reabsorption takes place there
Far fewer microvilli, as much less reabsorption takes place there
Cilia that sweep the filtrate along
questions.x: The PCT, where most reabsorption occurs, has a dense brush border of microvilli. DCT cells have few microvilli because they reabsorb a much smaller amount, under hormone control.

questions.q: The main component of normal urine is:
questions.x: Urine is mostly water, about 95%. Urea is the main dissolved waste, with salts and smaller amounts of uric acid and creatinine.

questions.q: After the fusion step in monoclonal antibody production, each hybridoma clone is tested (screened) in order to:
o: Remove the antigen from the mouse
Find the clone that makes antibody against the required antigen
questions.x: The B cells from the spleen make many different antibodies, so clones are screened and only the one producing antibody to the chosen antigen is grown on a large scale.

questions.q: The only human disease that has so far been eradicated worldwide through vaccination is:
questions.x: After a global vaccination campaign, smallpox was declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980. Polio still persists in a few countries, including Pakistan.

questions.q: In some early gene therapy trials, a few patients developed leukaemia. The main reason was that:
o: The inserted gene coded for a cancer-causing toxin
The viral vector inserted the gene next to a gene controlling cell division and switched it on
The patients were given too much insulin
The liposomes caused the white cells to burst
questions.x: Retroviral vectors insert their DNA at random places in the chromosomes. In these cases the insertion activated a gene that controls cell division, leading to uncontrolled growth of white blood cells.

questions.q: At STP, a student compares 16 g of oxygen gas (O₂) with 14 g of nitrogen gas (N₂). Which statement is correct? (N = 14, O = 16)
o: The oxygen sample occupies the larger volume
The nitrogen sample contains more molecules
questions.x: 16 g O₂ = 16/32 = 0.5 mol and 14 g N₂ = 14/28 = 0.5 mol. Equal moles of gases have equal numbers of molecules and, at STP, each occupies 0.5 × 22.4 = 11.2 dm³.

questions.q: A student writes four claims about the yield of a preparation. Which claim is true?
o: The theoretical yield is measured by weighing the product
Percentage yield is theoretical yield divided by actual yield, times 100
A higher actual yield always means a higher percentage yield
For a pure, dry product, the actual yield cannot be greater than the theoretical yield
questions.x: The theoretical yield is the calculated maximum, so a pure dry product cannot exceed it. It is calculated, not weighed, and a larger actual mass at a larger scale need not mean a higher percentage.

questions.q: The quantum mechanical (wave-mechanical) model of the atom, from which the orbital concept comes, is based on the wave equation of:
questions.x: Schrödinger's wave equation, solved for the electron in an atom, gives the orbitals as regions of electron probability. Bohr used fixed circular orbits instead.

questions.q: Lines produced when excited electrons of hydrogen drop to n = 2 are seen in which part of the spectrum?
questions.x: Transitions ending at n = 2 form the Balmer series, which lies in the visible region. Those ending at n = 1 (Lyman) are ultraviolet.

questions.q: An electron with n = 4 and l = 0 is present in the:
questions.x: l = 0 means an s subshell (l = 1 p, 2 d, 3 f), and n = 4 gives the fourth shell, so it is 4s.

questions.q: How many molecules are present in 5.6 dm³ of any ideal gas at STP? (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Moles = 5.6/22.4 = 0.25 mol; molecules = 0.25 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.505 × 10²³. The 2.408 × 10²⁴ value comes from multiplying by 4 instead of dividing.

questions.q: Graphs of volume against absolute temperature are drawn for the same gas sample at two pressures, P₁ and P₂, where P₁ is higher than P₂. Which line is steeper?
o: The line at the higher pressure P₁
Both lines have the same slope
Neither, because both graphs are curves
The line at the lower pressure P₂
questions.x: At constant pressure V = (nR/P)T, so the slope nR/P is larger when P is smaller. Both graphs are straight lines through the origin.

questions.q: The excluded-volume constant b of a real gas is measured in:
questions.x: b is the excluded volume per mole, so it is measured in dm³ mol⁻¹. The units atm dm⁶ mol⁻² belong to the constant a.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonds between NH₃ molecules are weaker than those between H₂O molecules because:
o: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen
Nitrogen has more lone pairs than oxygen
NH₃ molecules are heavier than H₂O molecules
Nitrogen is more electronegative than oxygen
questions.x: N (3.0) is less electronegative than O (3.5), so the N–H bond is less polar and its H carries a smaller partial positive charge. N has one lone pair, O has two.

questions.q: Wet clothes dry faster when they are spread out than when folded because:
o: A larger surface area lets more molecules escape at the same time
Spreading raises the boiling point of water
Folding lowers the temperature of the water
Spreading increases the intermolecular forces in water
questions.x: Evaporation happens from the surface, so a larger exposed surface lets more water molecules escape per second.

questions.q: Which of the following is a crystalline solid?
questions.x: Sodium chloride has a regular, repeating arrangement of ions. Glass, rubber and pitch have no long-range order and are amorphous.

questions.q: Which statement about ionic crystals is NOT correct?
o: They conduct electricity well in the solid state
They conduct electricity when dissolved in water
questions.x: In the solid the ions are locked in place, so ionic crystals do not conduct; they conduct only when molten or in solution.

questions.q: For X ⇌ Y, the rate constants of the forward and reverse reactions are kf and kr. At equilibrium, Kc equals:
questions.x: At equilibrium, kf[X] = kr[Y], so Kc = [Y]/[X] = kf/kr.

questions.q: Fe³⁺ (yellow) + SCN⁻ ⇌ FeSCN²⁺ (blood red). When more Fe³⁺ ions are added, the colour of the solution:
questions.x: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, forming more red FeSCN²⁺.

questions.q: Elementary steps involving three particles (termolecular steps) are rare because:
o: The chance of three particles colliding at the same instant with proper orientation is very small
Three particles always repel each other
Three particles cannot form an activated complex
questions.x: A simultaneous, correctly oriented collision of three particles is very unlikely, so most mechanisms are built from unimolecular and bimolecular steps.

questions.q: Experiments show that a reaction is half order in X and first order in Y. Its overall order is:
questions.x: Overall order is the sum of the powers: ½ + 1 = 1.5. Orders can be fractional because they are found by experiment.

questions.q: At room temperature, only a small fraction of collisions between reactant molecules lead to reaction. The main reason is that:
o: Most molecules do not collide at all
Most colliding molecules have less energy than the activation energy
The activated complex is very stable
questions.x: Collisions are very frequent, but most have energy below Ea and are not effective. Lowering Ea or raising temperature increases the effective fraction.

questions.q: The heat capacity of an object is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of:
o: 1 g of the object by 1 K
1 mol of the object by 1 K
The object to its boiling point
questions.x: Heat capacity refers to the whole object (J K⁻¹). Per gram it is the specific heat capacity, and per mole the molar heat capacity.

questions.q: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ. How much heat is needed to decompose 50 g of CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.x: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹, so 50 g = 0.5 mol. Heat = 0.5 × 178 = 89 kJ absorbed.

questions.q: On an enthalpy level diagram for an exothermic reaction, the products are shown:
o: At the same level as the reactants
questions.x: In an exothermic reaction heat is given out, so the products have less enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.

questions.q: Which statement is true of every redox reaction?
o: At least one element changes its oxidation number
Oxygen is always one of the reactants
A gas is always given off
questions.x: Redox reactions need not involve oxygen, gases or acids, but electrons are always transferred, so some oxidation numbers must change.

questions.q: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391. What is ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)?
questions.x: Bonds broken: 945 + 3(436) = 2253 kJ. Bonds formed: 6 N–H = 6(391) = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ.

questions.q: Two atoms with electronegativities 3.0 and 0.9 form a bond. The electronegativity difference shows that the bond is:
o: A polar covalent bond with little ionic character
questions.x: The difference is 2.1, which is greater than about 1.7, the value that corresponds to roughly 50% ionic character. So the bond is mainly ionic.

questions.q: Which order of carbon–halogen bond energies is correct?
questions.x: As the halogen atom gets larger from F to I, the bond gets longer and the overlap poorer, so bond energy decreases from C–F to C–I.

questions.q: 2.4 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. What volume of oxygen at STP is used? (Mg = 24; 1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Moles of Mg = 2.4/24 = 0.1; O₂ needed = 0.1/2 = 0.05 mol; 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 2.24 dm³.

questions.q: Tin(II) chloride, SnCl₂, is commonly used as a reducing agent because:
o: Sn(+2) is readily oxidised to the stable Sn(+4) state
Sn(+2) is readily reduced to tin metal
Chloride ions in it are strong oxidising agents
Sn(+4) is less stable than Sn(+2)
questions.x: For tin, the +4 state is still the more stable one, so Sn²⁺ easily loses two electrons and reduces other species.

questions.q: What is the total number of electrons in a gaseous Fe³⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26)?
questions.x: A neutral Fe atom has 26 electrons; losing 3 leaves 23. Adding 3 to get 29 is the sign mistake, and 24 is the count for Fe²⁺.

questions.q: Which functional group is present in both aldehydes and ketones?
questions.x: Both contain C=O. In aldehydes it carries at least one hydrogen atom (–CHO); in ketones it lies between two carbon groups.

questions.q: The functional group –CONH₂ is characteristic of:
questions.x: –CONH₂ (a carbonyl joined to nitrogen) is the amide group, as in ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂. Amines have –NH₂ without the C=O.

questions.q: Head-on overlap forming the C–C σ bond in ethene involves which orbitals?
questions.x: Each carbon in ethene is sp² hybridised, and head-on overlap of one sp² orbital from each carbon forms the C–C σ bond. The unhybridised 2p orbitals form the π bond.

questions.q: A geminal dihalide is a compound in which:
o: The two halogen atoms are on neighbouring carbon atoms
Both halogen atoms are on the same carbon atom
The two halogen atoms are at opposite ends of the chain
The halogen atoms are on a benzene ring
questions.x: Geminal (gem-) dihalides have both halogens on one carbon, e.g. CH₃CHBr₂. Vicinal (vic-) dihalides have them on adjacent carbons.

questions.q: The –CHO group in benzaldehyde directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the:
questions.x: –CHO withdraws electrons from the ring (like –COOH and –NO₂), so it deactivates the ring and is meta-directing.

questions.q: In the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, the electrophile that attacks the ring is:
questions.x: FeBr₃ polarises Br₂ and takes Br⁻ to form FeBr₄⁻, releasing the electrophile Br⁺, which attacks the π electrons of the ring.

questions.q: Which pair of structures are resonance (contributing) structures?
o: The two Kekulé structures of benzene
questions.x: The Kekulé structures have the same atom positions and differ only in where the π electrons are. Ethanol and dimethyl ether are structural isomers; cis and trans forms are geometric isomers.

questions.q: Benzene is converted into acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃) by Friedel–Crafts acylation, and the product is then nitrated. The main nitration product is:
questions.x: The –COCH₃ group withdraws electrons from the ring, so it is meta-directing and the –NO₂ group enters position 3.

questions.q: Kekulé proposed a ring of alternate single and double bonds for benzene. Which fact about benzene does this structure fail to explain?
o: Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆
Benzene does not readily undergo addition reactions as alkenes do
Benzene contains six carbon atoms in a ring
Benzene burns to give carbon dioxide and water
questions.x: Three localised C=C bonds should make benzene add bromine as alkenes do, but it does not. The formula and ring are consistent with Kekulé's structure.

questions.q: In which compound is the chlorine atom bonded to a carbon that is attached to only one other carbon atom (a primary alkyl halide)?
questions.x: In 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl, the CH₂Cl carbon is bonded to one other carbon, so it is primary. 2-Chlorobutane and 2-chloropropane are secondary, and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is tertiary.

questions.q: In the phenol molecule, a lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom is:
o: Completely localised on the oxygen atom
Used to form a coordinate bond with hydrogen
Partly delocalised into the π electron system of the benzene ring
Transferred to the ring as a hydride ion
questions.x: Overlap of an oxygen lone pair with the ring π system spreads electron density into the ring. This makes the ring more reactive and strengthens the C–O bond.

questions.q: Phenol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 100 °C. The main product is:
questions.x: Sulphonation of phenol gives mainly the ortho isomer at room temperature but the para isomer, 4-hydroxybenzenesulphonic acid, at about 100 °C. The meta isomer is not a main product because –OH directs ortho/para.

questions.q: Trichloroethanal (chloral), CCl₃CHO, is more reactive than ethanal towards nucleophiles. This is because the –CCl₃ group:
o: Releases electrons and decreases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Makes the carbonyl carbon sp³ hybridised
Withdraws electrons and increases the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
Removes the hydrogen from the carbonyl carbon
questions.x: The three electronegative chlorine atoms pull electrons away, making the carbonyl carbon more δ+ and so more attractive to nucleophiles. Electron-releasing alkyl groups have the opposite effect.

questions.q: Cyclohexanone, C₆H₁₀O, is reduced with sodium borohydride. The product is:
questions.x: NaBH₄ reduces the ketone C=O to CH–OH, giving the secondary alcohol cyclohexanol. It does not remove the oxygen to give cyclohexane, and it does not open the ring.

questions.q: On controlled oxidation with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, which pair of alcohols gives an aldehyde and a ketone respectively?
questions.x: Primary propan-1-ol gives propanal (aldehyde); secondary propan-2-ol gives propanone (ketone). Tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised, and methanol gives an aldehyde.

questions.q: Ethanoic anhydride, (CH₃CO)₂O, is hydrolysed by water. The product is:
questions.x: (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O → 2CH₃COOH: adding water reverses the dehydration that formed the anhydride.

questions.q: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, one glutamic acid in each β-chain is replaced by valine, and the protein changes shape and works poorly. This shows that:
o: The amino acid sequence determines a protein's shape and function
Only the quaternary structure affects function
Peptide bonds are broken in the faulty protein
The haem groups alone decide the shape of the protein
questions.x: A change of one amino acid in the primary structure alters the folding and so the function. The peptide bonds are intact; only the sequence differs.

questions.q: The force of attraction between an adhesive and the surface it is applied to is called:
questions.x: Adhesion is attraction between different substances, here the glue and the surface. Cohesion is the attraction within the adhesive itself.

questions.q: Which of the following physical quantities is defined as a vector product of two vectors?
questions.x: Torque τ = r × F is a vector product. Work and power are scalar products, and kinetic energy is not a product of two vectors.

questions.q: A ball dropped onto a hard floor rebounds to a smaller height than it was dropped from. This shows that the collision with the floor is:
o: Inelastic, with relative speed of separation less than that of approach
Perfectly elastic, with equal relative speeds
Perfectly inelastic, with zero speed of separation
Elastic, with relative speed of separation greater than that of approach
questions.x: A lower rebound means the ball leaves the floor more slowly than it arrived, so kinetic energy is lost and the collision is inelastic. It is not perfectly inelastic, because the ball does bounce.

questions.q: How far away does a stone land if fired over level ground at 20 m s⁻¹ and 30° elevation? (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 60° = √3/2, no air drag)
questions.x: R = v² sin 2θ / g = 400 × sin 60° ÷ 10 = 40 × √3/2 = 20√3 m (about 34.6 m). 40 m would be the maximum range, at 45°.

questions.q: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration along a straight line. Its displacement–time graph is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A curve getting flatter with time
A curve (part of a parabola) getting steeper with time
questions.x: With uniform acceleration from rest, s = ½at², so s against t is a parabola whose slope (velocity) keeps increasing.

questions.q: 1 s after launch, a projectile's velocity has a horizontal component of 6 m s⁻¹ and a vertical component of 4 m s⁻¹ upward. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal component 2 s after launch is:
questions.x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal component stays 6 m s⁻¹ throughout. Only the vertical component changes.

questions.q: Two bodies are shown by straight lines on the same displacement–time graph. The body whose line is steeper has the:
questions.x: The slope of a displacement–time graph is velocity, so the steeper line belongs to the faster body. A straight line means zero acceleration for both.

questions.q: When a book presses down on a table top, which force forms the third-law partner of this push?
o: Downward pull of the Earth on the table
Upward push of the table on the book
Upward pull of the book on the Earth
questions.x: Action and reaction act between the same two bodies. The book pushes down on the table, so the table pushes up on the book.

questions.q: A 2 kg block is released from rest at the top of a rough slope 5 m high and reaches the bottom at 8 m s⁻¹. The energy dissipated as heat by friction is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: PE lost = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. KE gained = ½ × 2 × 8² = 64 J. Energy lost to friction = 100 − 64 = 36 J.

questions.q: A box of mass m is lifted to the same height h once slowly and once quickly. The gravitational potential energy gained is:
o: The same, mgh, in both cases
questions.x: Gravitational PE depends only on mass, g and height. The time taken affects the power needed, not the potential energy gained.

questions.q: A body has a gravitational potential energy of −50 J relative to a chosen reference level. This means that:
o: It has 50 J less mass than at the reference level
It will rise by itself to the reference level
50 J of work must be done on it to raise it to the reference level
questions.x: Negative PE means the body is below the reference level, so 50 J of work against gravity is needed to lift it up to the zero level.

questions.q: A disc of radius 0.3 m turns through 5 rad. How far does a point on its edge travel along its circular path?
questions.x: s = rθ = 0.3 × 5 = 1.5 m. Dividing 5 by 0.3 gives 16.7, which is wrong.

questions.q: Water flows into a tank at 2 kg s⁻¹ and drains out at 1.5 kg s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
o: The mass of water in the tank increases by 0.5 kg every second
The mass of water in the tank stays constant
The mass of water in the tank decreases by 0.5 kg every second
Water must be created inside the tank
questions.x: Mass is conserved: mass in − mass out = 2 − 1.5 = 0.5 kg each second, which is stored in the tank. The flow through the tank is not steady.

questions.q: Fluid drag on a solid body moving through a liquid arises mainly because:
o: The liquid pushes up on the body with a force equal to the weight of liquid displaced
The body loses mass by dissolving in the liquid
The layer of liquid touching the body is dragged along, and viscous forces between liquid layers resist the motion
The liquid pressure is the same on all sides of the body
questions.x: Liquid in contact with the body moves with it, and internal friction (viscosity) between this layer and the layers further away produces a force opposing the motion. The upthrust is a separate force, not drag.

questions.q: Warm honey flows out of a jar much more easily than cold honey. This is because:
o: The density of honey increases when it is warmed
Warming honey increases the friction between its layers
The viscosity of a liquid decreases as its temperature rises
Gravity acts more strongly on warm liquids
questions.x: The viscosity of liquids falls with rising temperature, so warm honey has less internal friction and flows more freely.

questions.q: Engineers designing aircraft, cars and pipelines usually have to deal with turbulent rather than laminar flow because:
o: Laminar flow can only happen in gases
At the speeds and sizes involved, most real flows are turbulent
Turbulent flow obeys Stokes' law exactly
questions.x: Most practical fluid flows and most resistance to motion in fluids involve turbulent conditions. Turbulence actually wastes energy, and Stokes' law applies only to laminar flow.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, light from a single source passes through two narrow slits. The two slits act as coherent sources because:
o: They are very close to the screen
Both receive light from the same source, so their phase difference stays constant
They let through light of different colours
They are lit by two separate lamps
questions.x: Both slits are lit by the same wavefront, so any change in the source affects both equally and their phase difference stays fixed. That is what makes them coherent.

questions.q: In a stationary sound wave in air, a displacement antinode is a point where the variation of pressure is:
questions.x: Where the air particles move most, the layers on both sides move together, so the air there is neither squeezed nor stretched and its pressure does not vary. Pressure nodes coincide with displacement antinodes.

questions.q: When a longitudinal wave travels along a slinky spring, each coil of the spring:
o: Moves steadily from the source to the far end
Moves up and down across the length of the spring
Moves back and forth along the length of the spring about its own position
Stays completely still while the wave passes
questions.x: In a longitudinal wave the coils vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, about their mean positions. Only the compressions, rarefactions and energy travel along the spring.

questions.q: A point P goes round a circle of radius 20 cm once every 6 s. It begins at one end of a diameter. How far from the centre is the foot of the perpendicular from P to that diameter 1 s later?
questions.x: In 1 s P turns through 360°/6 = 60°, so the projection is at r cos 60° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 cm. Using sin 60° gives 17.3 cm.

questions.q: A reference point turns at 10 rad s⁻¹ on a circle of radius 0.1 m. The greatest acceleration of its projection on a diameter equals the point's centripetal acceleration. Its value is:
questions.x: a(max) = ω²r = 10² × 0.1 = 10 m s⁻². Using ωr gives 1, which is the maximum speed in m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The bright and dark fringes seen in Young's double-slit experiment are produced by:
o: Reflection of light from the edges of the slits
Absorption of light by the screen
Superposition of light waves from the two slits
Refraction of light in the air
questions.x: Light from the two slits superposes on the screen: in-phase arrival gives bright fringes and opposite-phase arrival gives dark fringes.

questions.q: Using Q = heat supplied to a gas, W = work done by the gas and ΔU = change in internal energy, which set of values is impossible?
questions.x: The first law needs Q = ΔU + W. For 200 J in and 100 J of work out, ΔU must be +100 J, not +300 J; the other sets all satisfy Q = ΔU + W.

questions.q: 4200 J of heat is given to 0.5 kg of water (specific heat 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Its temperature rises by:
Common salt dissolves easily in water partly because water has a relative permittivity of about 80. This means that, in water, the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions is:
o: About 80 times stronger than in vacuum
About 80 times weaker than in vacuum
About 80² times weaker than in vacuum
questions.x: In a medium F = kq₁q₂/(εr r²), so the force is reduced by the factor εr. Water weakens the ionic attraction about 80 times, helping the ions separate.

questions.q: An electron gains 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ J of kinetic energy when it is accelerated from rest. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the potential difference it moved through is:
questions.x: V = K/e = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2 × 10⁴ V (20 kV). Multiplying gives a tiny meaningless value.

questions.q: Two equal positive point charges, each +q, are a small distance apart. Far away from the pair (at distances much larger than their separation), the field lines look like those of:
o: A single point charge of +2q, radiating outward
A uniform field between parallel plates
questions.x: From far away the pair acts like one charge of total value +2q, so the lines spread out radially, as from a single positive charge.

questions.q: The resistance of a semiconductor such as a thermistor decreases as its temperature rises because:
o: More charge carriers are set free at higher temperature
Its free electrons collide more often with atoms
questions.x: Heating releases many more free electrons (and holes) in a semiconductor; this rise in charge carriers outweighs the extra collisions, so resistance falls.

questions.q: A conductor whose current is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, at constant temperature, is called:
questions.x: A conductor that obeys Ohm's law (I ∝ V at constant physical conditions) is called ohmic, for example a metal wire at steady temperature.

questions.q: A 0.5 m wire carrying 2 A is placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field and feels a force of 0.3 N. The flux density is:
questions.x: B = F/(IL) = 0.3/(2 × 0.5) = 0.3 T. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 0.3 × 2 × 0.5, a different and wrong value.

questions.q: A 20 kW supply is sent at 1000 V through cables of total resistance 2 Ω. What percentage of the power is lost as heat in the cables?
questions.x: I = 20000/1000 = 20 A; loss = I²R = 400 × 2 = 800 W, which is 800/20000 = 4% of the power.

questions.q: A straight metal rod 1 m long moves at 10 m s⁻¹ through a uniform field of 0.05 T, with the rod, its velocity and the field mutually perpendicular. The emf between its ends is:
questions.x: Motional emf ε = BLv = 0.05 × 1 × 10 = 0.5 V.

questions.q: An inductor of (1/π) H has a reactance of 200 Ω. The frequency of the supply is:
A trivalent impurity atom such as boron, added to silicon to make p-type material, is called:
questions.x: A trivalent atom leaves a vacancy (hole) in a covalent bond that can accept an electron, so it is called an acceptor. Pentavalent atoms are donors.

questions.q: A surface lit by 6 eV photons releases electrons with up to 3.5 eV of kinetic energy. How much energy is needed just to free an electron from it?
questions.x: From hf = φ + KEmax, φ = 6 − 3.5 = 2.5 eV. Adding the two energies (9.5 eV) is the usual slip.

questions.q: As the quantum number n increases, the energy levels of the hydrogen atom:
o: Get closer together and approach zero energy
Get farther apart and approach zero energy
Get closer together and approach −13.6 eV
questions.x: Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, so the gaps between successive levels shrink as n grows and the levels crowd towards 0 eV, the ionisation limit.

questions.q: Which of the following changes the activity (decays per second) of a given radioactive sample?
o: The number of undecayed nuclei it contains
Combining it chemically with another element
questions.x: Activity = λN, so it depends on how many undecayed nuclei are present. Decay is spontaneous, so temperature, pressure and chemical state do not affect it.

questions.q: Residents of Block C are informed that the water supply will be shut off from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Thursday while workers replace the main pipe. Please store enough water on Wednesday night. Tankers will stand near the park gate for emergencies only. We regret the trouble and thank you for your patience. The main purpose of this notice is to:
o: Tell residents about a planned water shut-off and how to prepare for it
Ask residents to pay for a new main water pipe
Invite residents to a meeting near the park gate
Complain that residents of Block C waste water
questions.x: The notice gives the time of the shut-off and advises residents to store water. It asks for no payment, calls no meeting and makes no complaint.

questions.q: "Instead of answering the reporters directly, the official gave an evasive reply that told them nothing." The word 'evasive' means:
questions.x: An 'evasive' reply avoids giving a direct answer; 'instead of answering directly' and 'told them nothing' are the clues.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "Be quiet! The baby ___ in the next room."
questions.x: 'Be quiet!' shows the action is happening now, so the present continuous 'is sleeping' is needed.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "The new medicine works well. ___, it has a few side effects."
questions.x: The second sentence contrasts with the first, so a contrast word, 'However', is needed.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Bilal hopes ___ a heart surgeon one day."
questions.x: 'Hope' is followed by the to-infinitive.

questions.q: Which phrase is correctly hyphenated?
questions.x: A compound adjective before a noun is joined by a hyphen between its own parts only: well-known.

questions.q: The word 'crying' is a participle describing a noun, not a gerund, in:
o: The crying baby woke everyone in the house.
Crying will not solve your problem.
She hates crying in front of others.
He is ashamed of crying at the film.
questions.x: In the first sentence 'crying' describes 'baby', like an adjective; in the others it names an action and works as a noun, so it is a gerund.

questions.q: Which sentence says clearly that Sara, and nobody else, passed the test?
questions.x: 'Only' should stand next to the word it limits; placed before 'Sara', it means no one else passed. In the other positions it limits the verb or 'the test' instead.

questions.q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "Did you ____ my letter last week?"
questions.x: The correct spelling is 'receive': the rule is 'i before e except after c', so after 'c' it is 'ei'.

questions.q: Ali will get the scholarship only if he scores above 90%. Ali got the scholarship. Which statement must be true?
o: Everyone who scored above 90% got the scholarship
Ali was the only student to get the scholarship
questions.x: 'Only if' makes scoring above 90% a necessary condition, so anyone who got the scholarship must have met it. It does not say that every high scorer gets one.

questions.q: "Our family has always put toothpaste on burns, so it must be the right treatment." What is wrong with this reasoning?
o: It attacks the person instead of the argument
It draws a rule from too few cases
It treats a practice as correct only because it has been done for a long time
questions.x: A long tradition is not evidence that a treatment works. Whether a remedy is right must be judged by evidence, not by how long it has been used.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1, 2, 6, 12, 36, 72, ?
questions.x: The multipliers alternate x2 and x3: 1, 2, 6, 12, 36, 72. The next step is x3, so 72 x 3 = 216.

questions.q: It is known that some X are Y and some Y are Z. Which statement can be concluded with certainty?
questions.x: 'Some X are Y' can be turned round to 'some Y are X'. Two 'some' statements give no definite link between X and Z, and 'some Y are Z' does not mean every Z is Y.

questions.q: Junaid, Kashif and Luqman live in Lahore, Multan and Quetta, and drive black, silver and white cars, one each. The man from Multan drives the silver car. Kashif drives the white car. Luqman does not live in Multan. The driver of the black car lives in Lahore. Who lives in Quetta?
questions.x: Kashif's car is white, so he is not the Multan man; Luqman is not either, so Junaid lives in Multan and drives silver. Luqman then drives black and lives in Lahore, leaving Kashif in Quetta.

questions.q: The sign @ is defined so that x @ y means x × y + x. What is the value of (2 @ 3) @ 1?

Statement: A student fainted during morning assembly on a very hot day. Courses of action: I. Morning assemblies should be banned in all schools. II. The school should arrange shade and drinking water during assemblies on hot days. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Shade and water deal with the heat that caused the fainting. Banning assemblies everywhere because of one incident is extreme.

questions.q: Statement I: A hospital in Peshawar held a free eye camp. Statement II: A college in Lahore won a national debating competition. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
Both statements are effects of some common cause
questions.x: The eye camp and the debate win are unrelated events in different cities. Neither causes the other, and they share no common cause.

questions.q: Statement I: The college's water pump broke down on Monday morning. Statement II: Hostel students could not get water for bathing on Monday. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: With the pump broken, water could not reach the hostel. The breakdown came first and produced the shortage.
